item.title: SSC Results: Pass rate, GPA-5 both decline in Chattogram Board
item.description:
The pass rate in this year’s Secondary School Certificate (SSC) examinations under the Chattogram Education Board is 59.48 per cent while, a total of 9,698 students achieved GPA-5.

Compared with last year, both the pass rate and the number of students achieving GPA-5 have declined.

The pass rate was 72.7 per cent last year, while 11,843 students had achieved GPA-5.

Examinations controller Parvez Sazzad Chowdhury disclosed the figures at the Chattogram Education Board auditorium at 10:00 am today, Monday.

Students from Chattogram, as well as Cox’s Bazar, Rangamati, Bandarban and Khagrachhari districts, sit for examinations under the Chattogram Education Board.

SSC results: 116,676 achieve GPA-5 as girls outshine boys

A total of 130,682 candidates registered for this year’s SSC examinations under the Chattogram Education Board. Of them, 130,219 appeared for the examinations.

A total of 77,453 students passed. The pass rate among boys is 58.76 per cent, while that among girls is 60.03 per cent. Girls had a slightly higher pass rate than boys also last year.

An analysis of the results shows that the pass rate in Chattogram city is 74 per cent. Last year, the rate was 81.03 per cent. Excluding the city, the pass rate in Chattogram district this year is 57.13 per cent, compared with 71.29 per cent in the last year.

Outside Chattogram city, the pass rate also declined in the four other districts under the board. In Cox’s Bazar, the pass rate is 57.3 per cent this year, compared with 70.76 per cent last year. In Rangamati, it is 41.17 per cent, down from 56.55 per cent.

In Khagrachhari, the pass rate fell to 34.99 per cent from 60.77 per cent. In Bandarban, it is 47.88 per cent this year, compared with 63.12 per cent last year.

By group, the pass rate is 84.41 per cent in the science group. The pass rate is 60.12 per cent in commerce group and 38.79 per cent in humanities group.

SSC Results: Zero pass rate in 312 institutions

School-wise results are also worse this year than last year. This year, all students passed in 21 schools compared with 33 such schools last year. On the other hand, no student passed in eight schools this year, compared with just one school last year.

This year’s SSC and equivalent examinations began on 21 April. The written examinations under the general education boards ended on 20 May.

SSC and equivalent examination results are usually published within 60 days of the end of the written examinations. Accordingly, the results were expected to be published on 20 July. However, they were published today, 10 August, nearly three weeks after the scheduled date.

item.description:

This means nearly 59 out of every 100 students who took the examinations in the department failed.
The findings emerged from an analysis of the 2026 SSC and equivalent examination results published on Monday.
Education Minister Dr ANM Ehsanul Haque Milon officially inaugurated the results at the Ministry of Education's conference room at 10am. Chairmen of all education boards subsequently handed over the results to the education minister.
Among the three departments under the nine general education boards, the humanities department recorded the lowest pass rate among boys. The pass rate for girls in the department was considerably higher at 54.38%, meaning around 46 out of every 100 female humanities students failed.
The gap between the pass rates of boys and girls in the humanities department was 13.24 percentage points, with girls performing significantly better.
Department-wise results show much stronger performance in the science stream. The pass rate among boys in science was 77.39%, compared with 83.70% among girls. In business studies, the pass rates were 59.98% for boys and 69.92% for girls.
Girls outperformed boys in all three departments, with the largest gender gap recorded in the humanities department. The department also had the lowest pass rate among boys.
The overall pass rate also declined this year. Across the nine general education boards, the average pass rate was 64.05%, down from 68.04% last year—a decline of 3.99 percentage points.
Among the general education boards, Dhaka recorded the highest pass rate at 71.63%, followed by Jessore at 66.27%, Comilla at 65.42%, Rajshahi at 63.67%, Barisal at 60.35%, Chittagong at 59.48%, Sylhet at 58.33%, Dinajpur at 58.05% and Mymensingh at 57.39%.
Across all education boards, including madrasa and technical boards, the overall pass rate in the SSC and equivalent examinations was 62.25%, compared with 68.45% last year—a decline of 6.20 percentage points.
A total of 116,676 students secured GPA-5 this year, compared with 139,032 last year. The number of GPA-5 achievers therefore fell by 22,356 in a year.
The results highlight both the particularly low pass rate in the humanities department and the significant gap between the performance of boys and girls in the stream.

item.title: India-Bangladesh relations plagued by Sheikh Hasina’s voice
item.description:
The short press conference held by former prime minister Sheikh Hasina in the Indian capital, Delhi, was supposed to be “irrelevant.” The opposite happened.
On the one hand, Hasina’s speech and brief question-and-answer session received extensive international media coverage. On the other, the Bangladesh government reacted strongly, protesting the conference held on August 5. Meanwhile, the Indian government distanced itself from the event, saying it had no involvement.
Although the Indian government tried to distance itself from Hasina’s speech, the incident has further strained relations between the two countries before they had a chance to recover. Whether there were any real signs of an improvement in relations even before Hasina’s speech, however, remains debatable. Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi has reportedly been waiting for more than a month for a courtesy meeting with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.
Bangladesh’s strong demand to India was that Hasina be prevented from making political statements. India, however, apparently decided not to deprive its protected guest of her freedom of speech, despite concerns that doing so could negatively affect bilateral relations.
Perhaps, from India’s perspective, bilateral relations did not have much room to deteriorate further. After coming to power, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman did not take any major steps to improve relations with Delhi. Relations had reached a low during the Yunus-led interim government and remained strained during Tarique Rahman’s first six months in office.
By allowing Hasina to hold a press conference despite Bangladesh’s strong objections, Delhi may have sought to convey to Dhaka that it remains interested in improving relations with Bangladesh, but not at the cost of abandoning Hasina.
Bangladesh’s response, meanwhile, came through a press release rather than a diplomatic note summoning the Indian high commissioner. Press releases are primarily intended for domestic audiences. However, such a statement was also necessary to counter the extensive international coverage of Hasina’s remarks. There is little doubt that Delhi will also assess Dhaka’s position based on that response.
It is difficult to say how far the repercussions of the incident will go or how long they will last.
Bangladesh’s State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed said Delhi would have to decide what kind of relationship it wants with Dhaka in the coming days. In reality, however, Bangladesh may have to make the first move.
The next summit of BRICS — comprising Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa — is due to be held in Delhi in a month. As the host country, India has invited Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to the summit’s outreach programme.
Even before Hasina’s speech, some were advising Tarique Rahman not to travel to Delhi. Following the speech, that advice could turn into a demand.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, however, invited Tarique Rahman to visit India with his family in February. Tarique Rahman did not accept the invitation for a bilateral state visit and instead travelled to China. There is little doubt that India took note of that decision.
The question now is what Tarique Rahman will do in the aftermath of Hasina’s speech. Bangladesh cannot simply say that “India has to decide.” At the very least, the BRICS invitation will have to be answered within the next two or three weeks.
The language used by the government in its reaction has also placed Dhaka in a difficult position, leaving limited room to change course. If Tarique Rahman accepts the invitation, he could face pressure from hardliners within his own party. If he declines, Bangladesh’s diplomacy could be viewed as immature in the international arena.
While there are domestic political reasons for the government’s strong reaction to Hasina’s speech, it is important to demonstrate diplomatic maturity in the larger national interest.
At the same time, it would not be surprising if Indian policymakers take steps to cool tensions by reassessing the situation.
Bangladesh’s new government, not yet six months old, had hoped to strengthen its claim to the political legacy of the “July Movement” by marking the second anniversary of Sheikh Hasina’s fall amid the 2024 protests. BNP policymakers were likely viewing the anniversary as an opportunity to establish party chairman and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman as a leading figure of the movement.
But Hasina, thousands of kilometres away in Delhi, has complicated those plans.
A few days before August 5, reports emerged that Hasina would address foreign journalists at the Foreign Correspondents Club (FCC) in Delhi. Speculation immediately followed: Would she appear in person, by video or through an audio link? Would she simply deliver a speech, or would there be a question-and-answer session?
It was clear that the Bangladesh government would not welcome any event involving Hasina on August 5.
Prime Minister’s Foreign Affairs Adviser Humayun Kabir reportedly asked Indian High Commissioner Dinesh Trivedi to prevent Hasina’s event, warning that her speech could have a negative impact on bilateral relations. His remarks were subsequently promoted on social media as a “strong message.”
The Indian government sought to distance itself from the FCC event, saying the club is a private institution and that the government has no authority to interfere in its professional activities.
Observers in Bangladesh were unconvinced, and perhaps for good reason.
It is true that the Indian government does not control the FCC’s activities and that the club does not require government permission to hold its events. But it is also true that the Indian government could have sought to postpone the event on grounds of law and order or national interest had it wanted to do so.
Instead, it allowed the event to proceed, sending a message to the Bangladeshi government.
Hasina did not simply attend the event on August 5 and deliver a speech. She effectively turned it into a mini-press conference, answering several questions from journalists present.
There was little new in her remarks. She had already said in a Reuters interview a few weeks earlier that she intended to return to Bangladesh in December.
The Delhi event reinforced her position that she had no contact with the Bangladesh government and intended to return home regardless of what the government did.
However, listening to Hasina and her son Sajeeb Wazed’s remarks, it appeared that they had taken the position that as long as those responsible for the deaths of hundreds of Awami League workers and supporters and around 50 police officers during the 2024 violence were given “immunity,” they would also demand immunity for those responsible for the deaths of protesters during the July-August movement.
The Yunus government granted immunity through an ordinance for crimes committed in connection with the movement, which was subsequently approved by the new parliament.
“The day this immunity is withdrawn, the day those responsible for the killing of police officers and Awami League leaders and activists are arrested, the Awami League will also apologise and express regret,” Sajeeb Wazed said in response to a question about whether the Awami League would apologise for killings committed during the 2024 movement.
At the same time, they spoke of reconciliation, resolving disputes and establishing peace. But no clear explanation was offered as to how reconciliation could be achieved politically while maintaining a hard-line position on the victims of the violence.
The current Bangladesh government regards former prime minister Sheikh Hasina as a “fugitive accused.” It is therefore angry that India allowed her to hold a press conference in Delhi.
But how does India view Hasina?
A comment by a former Indian diplomat offers some insight.
Former Indian high commissioner to Bangladesh Riva Ganguly Das told German broadcaster Deutsche Welle: “Sheikh Hasina came to India as a former prime minister. She did not run away; she did not come at midnight; she did not come in disguise; she was given to India by her country’s military for her safety.”
The account is not entirely without basis.
On August 5, 2024, a Bangladesh Army transport aircraft flew Hasina from Tejgaon Military Airport to the Indian Air Force’s Hindon base near Delhi. An investigative report by a Dhaka newspaper said a team of Special Security Force personnel assigned to Hasina’s security was also aboard the aircraft.
Dhaka-Delhi relations were among the many casualties of the fall of Hasina’s Awami League government amid widespread protests two years ago.
Relations deteriorated further during the 18 months of the interim government led by Grameen Bank founder Muhammad Yunus. There was some hope that relations would improve after the BNP won the February election, but that process has yet to gain momentum.
The question is: Who is more interested in improving relations? Which country can afford to turn its back on the other?
The simple answer is that both countries could, but neither would be wise to do so.
Beyond Hasina, Bangladesh and India have a long list of important bilateral issues that require close relations and regular dialogue.
If Hasina’s presence in Delhi is indeed a serious concern for Dhaka, she herself has proposed a possible solution: She has said she will return to Bangladesh in December.
The Bangladesh government should allow her to return and ensure that she is treated according to the law — including detention, trial, appeals and bail, where applicable.
The government itself has repeatedly demonstrated that Sheikh Hasina remains relevant to Bangladeshi politics. If all cases against her are resolved through due legal processes, perhaps the country’s politics can begin moving towards normalisation and stability.
Sabir Mustafa, former head of BBC Bangla, is currently working as a freelance journalist and podcaster. Email : sabir.mustafa@gmail.com

item.title: SSC results: How to apply for re-scrutiny?
item.description:
Students seeking a review of their SSC and equivalent examination results can apply for re-scrutiny from Tuesday, according to instructions issued by the Dhaka Education Board.
Applications will remain open until August 17, said Dhaka Education Board Controller of Examinations Professor Jesmin Taslim Banu.
To apply for re-scrutiny, students must visit the designated website, enter their roll and registration numbers, select their education board from the dropdown menu and click the submit button. They must then provide a mobile phone number, which will receive an SMS once the re-scrutiny results are published.
Students can select one or more subjects for re-scrutiny and click the “Pay Fee” button. The fee is Tk150 per paper. For subjects with two papers, applications must be submitted for both papers.
The SSC and equivalent examination results were published at 10am on Monday, with the nationwide pass rate falling to 62.25%, down from 68.45% in 2025.

item.title: SSC results: Dhaka tops, Madrasa Board records lowest pass rate
item.description:
Dhaka Education Board recorded the highest pass rate among all education boards in this year’s SSC and equivalent examinations, with 71.63% of students passing.
The Bangladesh Madrasa Education Board recorded the lowest pass rate, at 55.49% in the Dakhil examinations, according to an analysis of the 2026 SSC and equivalent results published on Monday.
Education Minister Dr ANM Ehsanul Hoque Milon formally inaugurated the publication of the results at the Education Ministry’s conference room at 10am. The chairmen of all education boards handed over the results to the minister at the event.
Among the nine general education boards, the average pass rate stood at 64.05%, down from 68.04% last year, a decline of 3.99 percentage points.
After Dhaka, the Jessore Education Board recorded the second-highest pass rate at 66.27%, followed by Comilla Board at 65.42%.
The pass rate was 63.67% in Rajshahi, 60.35% in Barisal, 59.48% in Chittagong, 58.33% in Sylhet and 58.05% in Dinajpur.
Mymensingh recorded the lowest pass rate among the nine general boards, at 57.39%.
Outside the general education boards, the Madrasa Education Board recorded a 55.49% pass rate in Dakhil, while the Technical Education Board recorded 58.20% in the SSC (Vocational) and Dakhil (Vocational) examinations.
The gap between the highest pass rate, recorded by Dhaka Board, and the lowest, recorded by the Madrasa Board, was 16.14 percentage points.
A total of 1,829,485 students sat for the examinations this year, with 1,138,897 passing. A total of 116,676 students secured GPA-5, down from 139,032 last year — a decline of 22,356.

item.title: SSC results: 690,608 students fail
item.description:
A total of 690,608 students failed this year’s Secondary School Certificate (SSC) and equivalent examinations, accounting for 37.75% of all candidates.
A total of 1,829,485 students sat for the examinations, of whom 1,138,877 passed, according to the results published on Monday.
The overall pass rate stood at 62.25%, down from 68.45% in 2025, a decline of 6.20 percentage points.
Girls significantly outperformed boys in the pass rate. While 66.68% of female candidates passed, the rate among male candidates was 57.86%, giving girls an 8.82 percentage-point lead.
Of the total candidates, 917,694 were boys and 911,791 were girls. Despite 5,903 more boys appearing for the examinations, 6,07,939 girls passed, compared to 5,30,938 boys — a difference of 77,001.
Girls also led in GPA-5 results, with 63,896 girls securing the top grade compared to 52,780 boys, a difference of 11,116.
The gender gap was evident across all three groups under the nine general education boards.
In science, the pass rate was 83.70% among girls, compared to 77.39% among boys. In humanities, 54.38% of girls passed, compared to 41.14% of boys. In business studies, the rates were 69.92% for girls and 59.98% for boys.
The widest gap was recorded in humanities, where the female pass rate was 13.24 percentage points higher than the male rate.
The number of GPA-5 achievers also fell this year, from 139,032 in 2025 to 116,676, a decrease of 22,356.
Education Minister Dr ANM Ehsanul Haque Milon formally inaugurated the publication of the results at the Education Ministry’s conference room at 10am on Monday. The chairmen of all education boards handed over the results to the minister at the event.
